extracted.intended_audience: computer_science students, programmers, documentation authors, and journal referees
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria for literate programming (program exposition, module naming, commenting, user manuals, typesetting) and for refereeing academic papers; drawn from lecture notes and class critiques. Useful for authors of programs/manuals and referees of CS research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural order of exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Present program constructs to the reader using the same order in which the creator made decisions about them; there is a natural order of exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the ordering that felt natural during composition; reading and writing orders are similar. Structure documentation so the reader encounters concepts in the same decision sequence as the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of person (we/it/I)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to describe program behavior as autonomous or as involving the reader (e.g. 'we insert the element' vs 'it inserts the element'); be consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don favours 'we'; others prefer different conventions (and some favour anthropomorphizing with 'I'). Choose a viewpoint and apply it consistently throughout documentation and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module naming: imperatives vs descriptors
rubrics_metrics.description: Use imperatives for modules that perform actions (e.g., 'Store the word in the dictionary') and descriptors for declarative modules (e.g., 'Procedures for sorting').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the grammatical form of the module name to its function: verbs/imperatives for procedures, noun phrases/descriptors for lists of declarations or descriptive blocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module name capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: It is natural to capitalize the first letter of a module name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capitalize initial letter only; avoid capitalizing every word in module titles (don't use newspaper-headline-all-words-capitalized style). Prefer capitalizing only the first word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identifier readability (underscores / compound names)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a short underscore to conjoin words (e.g., get_word) for compound identifiers to improve printed readability; WEB removes the underscore for Pascal compatibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid awkward uppercase-after-lowercase like 'FindinNewWord3'. Use underscores or long descriptive identifiers; examples: Jim Dunlap used very long descriptive identifiers (40+ chars) with clear meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module description: high-level, informal, clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Each module should contain an informal but clear description of what it actually does; a play-by-play account of an algorithm does not qualify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a high-level intuition of the module's purpose and behavior rather than step-by-step execution. Aim to convey the idea rather than low-level mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module size / decomposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep modules short—Don thinks a dozen lines of code is about the right length; break long modules into manageable pieces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WEB philosophy: break complex things into tractable parts. If a module is too long, cut it into several pieces so the exposition mirrors modular decomposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'engineerese' and poor prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid writing that is all conjunctions and no punctuation (stream-of-engineerese); good documentation requires readable prose and proper punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write complete sentences, use punctuation, avoid stream-of-consciousness engineer jargon unless intentionally stylistic and carefully controlled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid carrying obsolete conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't carry excess baggage from older styles into new formats (e.g., adding comments after each end as in Pascal is unnecessary in WEB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adopting a new style or tool, drop conventions that are redundant or harmful in the new context; adapt to the conventions of the new system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anthropomorphization caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful about anthropomorphizing computer systems (prompt wording like 'Name of file to process?' versus 'What process?'); decide whether the program speaks as 'I' or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some prefer 'I' for clarity and user conceptualization; others (e.g., Dijkstra) disapprove. Either choice is acceptable if used consistently and with awareness of user perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not start sentences with symbols
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid beginning sentences with symbols (e.g., don't write 'data assumes that ...'); rewrite so sentences begin with words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure prose follows normal grammatical sentence structure for readability; rewrite expressions so symbols occur within sentences rather than as sentence-initial tokens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive variable naming / 'Truth in Naming'
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose descriptive variable names (e.g., caps_range instead of range); let the function determine part of speech: verbs for procedures, nouns for data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clarity over brevity; ensure names reflect purpose. Example: rename 'scan' (a verb) to 'place' or another noun if it's a placeholder/data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment variable declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: When declaring variables (in WEB you can do so at any point), add at least a brief comment explaining them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even cursory explanations near declarations help readers understand purpose and usage; this is especially important when declarations are distributed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typesetting conventions for math and code
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of typography: typeset asterisks may appear higher than typewritten ones; use 'x' for multiplication; use typewriter-style font for body-centered '.' and for certain data (like hex).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer x for multiplication in printed text; use typewriter font for hexadecimal numbers (e.g., '3F') while leaving decimal numbers in normal type to aid subliminal checking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep related routines grouped in exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep specialized data-structure routines (e.g., heap routines) together in the text so they can be read as a group while fresh in the reader's mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although WEB allows flexible ordering, group related operations conceptually to improve reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency between documentation and program wording
rubrics_metrics.description: The words used in the documentation should match the words used in the formal program; using two different terms for the same thing confuses readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain consistent terminology across comments, documentation, and code identifiers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of begins/ends inside called modules
rubrics_metrics.description: Put begins and ends inside the called modules rather than in the calling module; mixing the two conventions causes bugs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of correct style: define (Punt) = begin ... end and call as if down = 4 then (Punt); rather than embedding begin/end around the call. Mixing styles leads to bugs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate error handling from main flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid stuffing error handling inline so that the normal-case logic becomes obscured; use a short reference near the start that points to a separate error-handling module.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., put (Check if the data is wrong 28) in the main module and implement the error detection/recovery in module 28. This preserves focus on normal-case code and motivates writing good error routines separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use italics for variable names in comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use italics for names of variables when they appear in comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent typographic treatment (italics) helps distinguish program variables in explanatory prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Module-title parameters correspond to local parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: Let the variables in the module title correspond to the local parameters in the module itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The title should reflect the module's interface to make the exposition and code align closely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use technical terms accurately
rubrics_metrics.description: Use domain terminology correctly (e.g., don't label a program 'tail recursive' unless it actually uses tail recursion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid misuse of impressive-sounding phrases outside their proper context; incorrect usage misleads readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribute local variable declarations near use
rubrics_metrics.description: For large procedures, distribute local variables as the exposition proceeds and place declarations near their point of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This matches WEB's philosophy and improves readability; while Pascal may restrict this, in exposition distribute variable descriptions logically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use macros judiciously to improve language expressiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Macros can be used to simulate missing language features (e.g., define string_type(#) == packed array [1:#] of char to allow name_code : string_type(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use macros to work around language limitations (Pascal examples) but keep macros simple (Don's macros often allow only one parameter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid misleading or inconsistent quotations and punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware of differences between opening and closing quotes and conventions across languages; avoid inconsistent usage like 'main program' with wrong quote types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose a consistent ASCII representation for quotes if publishing in environments that lack typographic quotes; proofread examples carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cryptic capitalization and ALL-CAPS in manuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use all caps (e.g., 'ENTER') in user manuals as it looks like a danger sign; don't make naive claims about ease that may patronize users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use normal-case, short sentences, and friendly wording; avoid terminology that the naive user may not understand.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain jargon and UI terms for naive users
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms familiar to CS people (e.g., 'menu', 'scrolling', 'cursor') may be meaningless to naive users; define or replace them with plain-language alternatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use words like 'flashing bar' instead of 'cursor' or 'hit return' instead of 'enter' when targeting novices; prefer plain-language descriptions and short sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always explain how to exit or recover
rubrics_metrics.description: User manuals should always explain 'How do I get out of a mess if I do something wrong?'—explain how to exit or back out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include explicit, non-jargon instructions for stopping or undoing actions; do not assume the user can guess how to quit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide interactive demos or concise online help
rubrics_metrics.description: Inviting the user to type '?' for an online demonstration can spare long textual explanations and keep the manual terse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interactive examples or demos when appropriate; animated demonstrations or short interactive help reduce long textual descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sensible defaults and reduce repetitive prompts
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid prompting for many parameters repeatedly with fixed defaults; better to default to the style used for the preceding line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember user workflow; persistent defaults that reflect recent choices are more natural than fixed, repetitive defaults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design manuals to be easy to skim and visually clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Good manuals have a clear overview, step-by-step descriptions, crisp sentences, helpful redundancy, diagrams, and keyboard diagrams; they should be friendly and easy to skim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate that readers often start in the middle; use headings, diagrams, symbols for control keys, icons for scrolling, and highlight important actions like 'hold control while pressing another key'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use icons and diagrams to explain UI actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Icons to describe scrolling up/down/left/right and keyboard diagrams to indicate keys improve comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly indicate interactions (e.g., that 'up' means previous message) rather than assuming users will infer them; clarify ambiguous phrases like 'THIS IS VISIBLE HERE BUT NOT HERE'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: friendly encouragement vs patronizing claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Include encouraging comments like 'Good luck!' but avoid unhelpful or patronizing reassurances (e.g., 'this system has been carefully redesigned not to bite').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep tone encouraging and clear without false or condescending claims about usability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofreading and handling galley proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully review galley proofs and copy-editing changes; publishers may request additional bibliographic details (e.g., conference location/date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check editorial substitutions (word choices), correct errors introduced by copy editors, and supply requested bibliographic details; be aware that libraries index conferences by city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliography accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide accurate and sufficiently detailed bibliography entries; careless copying propagates errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify bibliographic details; Don notes many bibliographies contain errors and that authors often copy blindly—ensure correctness, including conference specifics if requested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing primary criterion: originality
rubrics_metrics.description: The first criterion for refereeing a paper should be originality: is the material a genuine advance on previous work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the submission contributes new results or insights beyond existing literature before considering other aspects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing technical quality and correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should detect subtle technical errors and assess overall technical quality; they can provide corrections or contribute results anonymously when helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check proofs, algorithms, and claims carefully; if necessary, implement or test code/algorithms to verify criticisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing completeness: algorithm, correctness argument, limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper should contain: (1) a complete algorithm, (2) a proof or convincing explanation of correctness, (3) a statement of limitations on the algorithm's applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these checklist items as core expectations for submissions of algorithmic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing: provide references to related work
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should provide references to related work the author may have missed and suggest relevant literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Help authors situate their work and improve technical context by suggesting prior art and related results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee attitude: be a teacher and give constructive criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees should view themselves as teachers whose role is to help authors improve their writing and results; avoid tasteless or mean comments under anonymity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offer constructive, actionable feedback rather than mere denunciation; remember the author may be an early-career researcher who will write more papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus reviews according to paper merit
rubrics_metrics.description: If content is clearly poor, prioritize major flaws over copyediting; if the paper has substantive merit, also ensure exposition quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate reviewer effort proportionally: correct critical technical issues first; if the paper is valuable, also help with clarity and presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose journals for reviewer quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should select journals with the best referees, not those with lenient editors; good referees help determine whether a real contribution exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize venues known for strong peer review to get meaningful feedback and to validate contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use structured review forms to prompt issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Asking referees to answer a specific list of questions may prompt consideration of issues they might otherwise forget.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structured checklists can improve review thoroughness; combine with space for freeform comments and overall rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referee ratings and filtering
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees are often asked to assign overall ratings (accept; accept with minor/major changes; reject) and to suggest alternative journals for rejected submissions, providing downward filtering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ratings to guide editorial decisions and to recommend more suitable venues when necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibrate referee quality via shared review
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor can calibrate referees by sending the same paper to multiple referees and comparing reports to identify reliable reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative evaluation of referee reports can reveal which referees give useful, constructive feedback vs. superficial or idiosyncratic reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of facile generalizations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid recommending or accepting generalizations that are merely mechanical, 'facile generalizations' that add no real insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage substantive, insightful extensions rather than trivial manipulations of arguments.
